message:
Redesign send and receive method sheets (#313)

* Let flow sheets slide out instead of vanishing

Closing any of the six flow sheets deleted it. Measured frame by frame on a
Pixel 7a, the sheet crossed the whole screen in 23ms over three frames — under
two frames of perceptible travel, which reads as the sheet being cut rather
than dismissed. Swipe-to-dismiss always looked right, which is the clue.

Material3 gives a sheet three motion specs. A drag settles through
`anchoredDraggableMotionSpec`, a spatial spring — that is the swipe. `hide()`
animates with `hideMotionSpec`, which BottomSheet.kt sets to `fastEffectsSpec`:
an effects spring at stiffness 3800, damping 1.0. Effects springs are tuned for
0..1 alpha. A sheet dismissal is a ~2400px translation, and at that stiffness it
is over before it is visible. Every close button, back press and scrim tap in
the app went through it.

So the sheet composes under a motion scheme that returns a spatial spring from
`fastEffectsSpec`, and its content composes under the real one. BottomSheet.kt
re-reads the spec on every recomposition, so overriding the value it reads is
the assignment that sticks — setting `hideMotionSpec` directly does not survive,
and would only have covered our own close lambda anyway, leaving back press and
scrim tap snapping. `fastEffectsSpec` is read in exactly one place in the whole
sheet implementation, so scoping the override to the sheet changes the dismissal
and nothing else.

Measured after, same method:

  close button   23ms / 3 frames  ->  166ms / 16 frames
  back press     23ms / 3 frames  ->  163ms / 16 frames
  swipe          unchanged (settles through the spatial spec it always used)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Say what a mint amount rejection actually means

CDK's error text for a NUT-04/05 limit rejection was reaching the UI
verbatim, and it always reads "Amount must be between `0` and `0` is
`0`". The zeros aren't a bug in the mint's response: the mint returns
code 11006 with the real bounds in `detail`, but cdk-common's
`From<ErrorResponse> for Error` rebuilds the variant from the numeric
code alone, filling all three fields with `Amount::default()`. The
message can never say anything but zero, for any mint at any amount.

The classifier already had a rule for this case; its needles just never
matched CDK's own wording, so the message fell through to the raw-string
fallback. Match the phrasing CDK actually emits.

`TransactionUnbalanced` is zeroed by the same decoder and no rule caught
it at all, so a rejected swap rendered as "Inputs: `0`, Outputs: `0`,
Expected Fee: `0`". Map that too.

Both matchers take their needles from the `#[error(...)]` attributes in
cdk-common so they track the wording that actually ships, and both
platforms carry parity tests that fail if the strings drift again.

Payment facts on the pay/receive terminal and its confirm screen showed
an SF Symbol / Material glyph beside each field label. The transaction
receipt dropped those in 27e78a27; the payment flow kept them, so the
same Method/Amount/Network fee/Mint rows read two different ways.

Strip the leading glyph from the two-column row vocabulary on both
platforms: PaymentStatusView.DetailRow loses its icon field, and the
confirm/detail rows feeding into it (melt, Cashu request, receive
Lightning, receive token, generated ecash) follow. Android's
InspectorRow keeps its leadingIcon parameter for Settings and mint
detail, which are a different surface.

Trailing affordances stay — the pencil on editable rows, the outbound
link arrow, the seal/caution glyph qualifying a locked-ecash key, and
the mint chevron. Method/action rows keep their icons: there the glyph
names a destination, not a field.

Recorded as The Iconless-Row Rule in DESIGN.md and UX_SPEC.md.

Fix Android UI retry temp-file portability (#312)

Type amounts as whole numbers, with a decimal key (#307)

Entering "21" on a USD mint produced $0.21. The keypad was a minor-unit
accumulator: every digit shifted in from the right, so the raw string always
carried a full fraction and "21" meant twenty-one cents. Anyone paying $21
sent 21c, and the wrong value reached the mint.

Digits now build the integer part left to right, and the decimal key — in the
bottom-left slot that was already a blank spacer — arms the fraction. One
grammar, shared by both platforms:

    raw  := "" | INT | INT "." | INT "." FRAC
    INT  := "0" | [1-9][0-9]{0,11}
    FRAC := [0-9]{0,decimals}

The trailing "." is the "fraction armed" state, so no screen needs a new flag
beyond the String it already holds, and none of the 9 iOS or 5 Android call
sites changed. sat units render no decimal key at all: sats are indivisible
here, so a fraction could only produce a rounding surprise.

The load-bearing change is the parser. entryBaseUnits threw the separator away
and called every remaining digit a minor unit, which only worked because the
accumulator guaranteed a full fraction. It is now decimal-position aware on
both platforms — this is what every mint quote, melt quote and sendTokens call
reads.

Two live iOS bugs sat inside the rewritten functions and are fixed here:

  - sat entry had no cap. `raw + key` ran forever and `UInt64(raw) ?? 0` then
    returned 0, so holding a key silently zeroed the amount.
  - the fiat cap was checked before the *10, letting the value land ten times
    past it. Android clamped correctly; the two had drifted.

Also collapses iOS's two identical accumulators into one (fiat is just a
two-decimal unit, as it already is on Android), and makes the raw separator
canonical "." on both platforms with the locale separator applied at display
time. That last one fixes a latent collision on comma-decimal locales, where
grouping 1234 as "1.234" and appending ".5" gave "1.234.5".

Send-screen fixes surfaced by the new model:

  - The insufficient-balance notice was a sibling of the amount, so it shoved
    the hero upward the instant it appeared — ~310px on Send Ecash, ~60px on
    Unified Send with no transition at all. Both now use iOS SendView's
    layout: one flexible cell, amount centred, notice overlaid at its bottom.
    Under the old model "21" was $0.21 and never tripped the warning, which is
    why this went unnoticed.
  - The notice drops its detail line (the balance is on the mint row directly
    above), loses its tonal container, and centres under the amount.
  - Send Ecash's header showed a back chevron that re-presented the Send
    sheet — it is swapped into the sheet, not pushed onto it, so leaving slid
    the Send sheet back in behind the user. It closes to the wallet now, and
    the glyph says so. The result faces really do step back and keep the arrow.

PendingOrange was Material Orange 800 and caution text was a pale cream
(#FFDCB0) that barely read as orange. Repointed to Apple's systemOrange, the
way ReceivedGreen is already systemGreen — only the orange had drifted.
Dark carries systemOrange itself (10.2:1 on canvas, 7.1:1 on container);
light keeps a darkened same-hue variant because #FF9500 on white is 2.2:1.

Tests: shared entry vectors on both platforms, new keypad and hero goldens,
and a bare+centred notice added to the inline-notice catalog.

Re-arm the QR scanner whenever its camera surface reappears (#301)

A consumed scan sets the intake latch to "not scanning", and it was only
restored on the inline-reject timer. Any appearance path that doesn't
rebuild the scanner state — a cancelled interactive sheet dismissal, a
stacked confirm cover closing, SwiftUI reusing retained sheet state, or a
Compose composition surviving an exit-animation reversal — left a live
camera preview that silently dropped every subsequent scan until the
scanner was closed and reopened.

iOS: QRScannerViewController.viewWillAppear now reports through the
scanner delegate and ScannerWrapperView resets the scan model, so a
visible scanner is always an armed scanner.

Android: the shell bumps a scanner session id per opening and the scan
state (completed latch, animated-QR progress and decoder) is keyed to it,
so a reused composition re-arms on reopen.

Skip clipboard auto-receive for spent tokens on iOS and Android (#302)

Tapping Receive auto-pasted any Cashu token found on the clipboard, and
the typed-input auto-route then skipped the receive sheet straight to
the claim page — even when the token was already spent, where the claim
only failed after tapping Receive. While a spent token sat on the
clipboard, every Receive tap got hijacked and nothing else (Cashu
Request, Lightning, scan) could be started from the sheet.

Gate the auto-paste on the existing NUT-07 spent check
(checkTokenSpent): a confirmed-spent clipboard token leaves the input
empty and shows a caution hint instead. When the check can't run
(offline, unreachable mint, undecodable token) the token is pasted
anyway and the claim page surfaces its own error. Manual paste, scans,
and deep links keep routing immediately without the extra round-trip.

Adds a TokenParser.mintUrl helper on both platforms that decodes only
the mint URL without expanding proofs (proofsSimple() can fail for IDv2
keysets), plus unit tests for the paste/suppress decision.

Resume, don't restart, the Android UI suite when the emulator dies (#303)

The managed-device runs have been failing at a deterministic point: the
emulator expires ~6 minutes into the suite (test #56 of 89 records an
empty failure and a 40-50s hang, logcat cuts off mid-test, adb reports
'device offline', the remaining 33 tests never run). The failure point is
invariant to which tests run and what they render. The retry script then
re-ran all 89 tests from scratch, re-cooking each fresh emulator to the
same crash — attempts failed identically three times in a row.

On a transient mid-run death, collect the test classes that completed
cleanly from the Gradle result XML and retry with the runner's notClass
filter excluding them: attempt two resumes where the suite died instead
of restarting it, so a single ~6-minute emulator lifetime no longer fails
the job. A genuinely failing class is never excluded (it carries a
failure record), real assertion failures still skip the retry path
entirely, and the ledger unions across attempts.
chore: set app version to 0.3 on iOS and Android (#300)

Update CDK bindings to v0.18.0-rc.0 and adopt native transaction lifecycle + NUT-16 (#298)

Deps: cdk-swift/cdk-android 0.17.3-rc.0 -> 0.18.0-rc.0 (iOS SPM pins, Xcode
project, CI IntegrationTests package, Android libs.versions.toml). The app
workspace Package.resolved is now committed (un-ignored): ios-tests.yml keys
its dependency cache on that file, so an untracked pin made CI restore a
stale cached cdk-swift clone and fail resolution with -skipPackageUpdates.

Breaking-change migrations (both apps):
- Keyset APIs consolidated: refreshKeysets()/getMintKeysets(filter)/
  getActiveKeyset() -> keysets(policy:)/activeKeyset()/keyset(id) returning
  full KeySet records (mapped to KeySetInfo where Token.proofs needs it).
- MintQuote/quote response records gained updatedAt/method/counters; manual
  quote construction sites updated.
- WalletConfig/WalletRepositoryConfig gained optional rateLimit (default
  pacing left enabled; CDK now paces mint requests client-side).

Transaction lifecycle: CDK 0.18 records every send/receive/mint/melt with a
stable saga-derived transaction id and a native pending/completed/failed
status, replacing the apps' hand-rolled pending tracking:
- History maps CDK status directly instead of hardcoding Completed and
  fuzzy-merging local token stores by (mint, amount, closest timestamp).
  Sent-token strings are keyed by transaction id (savedTokens), with a
  saga-JSON backfill for pre-upgrade sends.
- Unpaid/expired invoice rows are still synthesized from unissued mint
  quotes (a quote has no transaction until minting starts), now skipping
  any quote CDK already owns a transaction for and preferring the quote's
  native updatedAt over the local first-seen map.
- Pending sends: getPendingSends()/checkSendStatus(operationId) replace
  checkProofsSpent-based PendingToken/ClaimedToken polling; revokeSend()
  replaces receive-back reclaim (deleted; no UI callers remain).
- Pending melts (NUT-05 async): local pendingMeltQuotes/preimage/fee
  bookkeeping deleted; CDK's durable saga + recoverIncompleteSagas()
  reconcile on startup and in the foreground poll.
- Paid-but-unissued mints: per-quote backoff/throttle machinery
  (MintQuoteCheckBackoff, in-flight sets, BOLT12 amountPaid/amountIssued
  heuristics) replaced by wallet.mintUnissuedQuotes() sweeps; per-quote
  refresh uses native amountPaid > amountIssued (amountMintable) counters.
- Detail-screen row resolution shrunk to a 3-line liveDetail(openId,
  openQuoteId) helper on both platforms (quote-id fallback for the
  quote-row -> saga-tx-row swap); the dedicated lookup files with their
  completed-then-newest tie-breakers are deleted.
- Obsolete UserDefaults/DataStore keys are purged once at launch and stay
  on the wallet-deletion wipe lists.

NUT-16 animated QR: hand-wired BC-UR stacks replaced by CDK's
TokenUrEncoder/TokenUrDecoder on both platforms:
- QR display (QRCodeView) emits CDK fountain-encoded ur:bytes frames for
  long Cashu tokens; non-token payloads stay single static frames.
- Scanner reassembly (iOS ScannerViewModel, Android AnimatedUrDecoder)
  delegates to CDK's TokenUrDecoder; progress tracks fountain-resolved
  fragments.
- URKit (iOS) and bcur-kotlin (Android) dependencies removed.
- Round-trip coverage: Android instrumented tests
  (AnimatedUrDecoderInstrumentedTest, QRCodeViewInstrumentedTest); Swift
  round-trip verified live against the 0.18 bindings.

Verified: iOS app + unit tests + live-mint integration suites (Nutshell &
CDK) + UI tests pass; Android app + 590 unit tests pass; send/claim/revoke,
mintUnissuedQuotes, and NUT-16 encode/decode verified end-to-end against
live mints/bindings.

* iOS: extract the fixed onboarding chassis, make all 8 steps stages

Onboarding restyle stage 1 (docs/product/onboarding-restyle-brief.md §3, §9).
One persistent OnboardingChassisView is pinned via safeAreaInset on the
onboarding root; every step's headline, subhead, and CTA stack moved into a
per-step OnboardingChassisModel, and the step switch now swaps stage-only
views above it. Absent secondary/tertiary actions render hidden template
buttons so the primary CTA's frame is identical on every step (the brief's
success criterion), tracked by the new testPrimaryCtaFrameConstantAcrossSteps.

Zero new motion: the chassis is shielded from the step-change animation with
a transaction override; value-scoped feedback (press, enable/disable fades,
the acknowledge checkbox, the iCloud staged exit) still animates. Error
banners moved into the stages so they can never displace the primary CTA.
Every accessibility identifier stays on the same logical control; all
disabled-until-valid rules, branch paths, and documented anti-patterns
(unanimated seed grid, redacted+blur masking, mnemonic snapshot) are
preserved verbatim.

Onboarding restyle stage 1 groundwork. Each restore step now exposes a

* Apply the shared onboarding motion spec on both platforms

* Welcome stage: the "note becomes cash" ink piece (both platforms)

Onboarding restyle stage 3 (brief §4) — the direction Erik picked. A
thin-stroke banknote outline slowly closes into an ecash-token circle while
two MintAvatar-sized companion circles resolve beside it: a note becoming
digital cash, in pure ink. No gradient, illustration, fill, shadow, or brand
mark; system-semantic strokes only.

iOS (OnboardingWelcomeStage): one autoreversing SwiftUI animation (~3.2s each
way) — animation-driven, never timer-driven, so UITEST_DISABLE_ANIMATIONS
freezes it deterministically. Android (WelcomeStagePiece): one autoreversing
infinite transition with every animated value read inside drawBehind, so the
loop costs zero recompositions and a cold launch's first frame can't stutter.
Reduce Motion holds the composed token-cluster end state on both platforms;
the piece is decorative and hidden from accessibility. The restore-method
chooser gets the static quiet variant at half opacity.

Prototype pending Erik's still-frame sign-off before polish (brief §4).

* Onboarding: the handoff erodes instead of sliding

The curtain's exit was a 20pt slide-down plus a uniform fade, which read
as a cut. Lifting the whole plane a screen height instead only traded one
problem for another: a rigid rectangle travelling that far is a slide
transition, and feathering its edges cannot disguise that. A travelling
edge is no better — that is a wipe.

So nothing translates now and no edge moves. The curtain dissolves by its
own material. The renderer already buckets cells by level and draws five
batches, so per-level opacity costs one draw-state change per bucket: the
batching that makes the field cheap is exactly what lets it erode. Three
things run off one progress value. The opaque scrim clears early (42%),
so the wallet stands up behind a terrain that is still substantially
there — the reveal is a change of material, not a change of screen. The
glyphs then dissolve level by level through staggered, overlapping,
smoothstepped windows: the faint dotted plain thins first, the contour
ridgelines hold, and the ₿ peaks are the last things standing over the
balance. A top bias with fixed geometry and animating strength clears the
field top-down. The only motion is the field's own drift and the bloom's
release swirl unwinding underneath — motion that was already there rather
than motion imposed on the plane.

1000ms on a linear driver: every stage carries its own smoothstep, so
easing the driver too would double-ease the dissolve and stall it mid-way.

* Onboarding: enter the seed phrase one word at a time

were in. It now asks for one word at a time and validates each as it lands: a

* Onboarding: the rail scrub works under an actual thumb

The press-and-hold scrub shipped wired to SwiftUI's LongPressGesture
sequenced into a DragGesture. Inside a ScrollView that sequence falls apart
on a real device: the scroll view's pan steals the drag half the moment the
finger moves, so the hold engaged and then nothing tracked. The simulator
suite never noticed because no test ever synthesized the gesture — it only
ever tapped.

The rail's touch handling drops to UIKit, where this interaction is native:
one UILongPressGestureRecognizer is press-and-hold-then-track-movement by
design, recognizers see touches regardless of the scroll view's content-
touch delays, and a recognized hold locks the scroll pan out for the rest
of the touch. Hold still a quarter second and the scrub engages; move early
and it scrolls as normal. allowableMovement is raised to 24pt because a
resting thumb wobbles past the 10pt default and would silently fail the
hold, and the surface reaches 10pt past the rail on every side so engaging
doesn't require landing on a 24pt strip.

The tick Buttons are gone — taps ride the same surface through a tap
recognizer, which leaves iOS structurally identical to Android's container-
level detectors. If the hold starts on the already-focused word the
engagement tick comes from the rail itself, never doubled with onSelect's.

press, hold, drag top to bottom — and asserts the rail lands on word 12,
the keyboard survives, and a plain tap still jumps. The interaction that
broke silently can't again.

Third pass on the same jank, and the real lesson. The sequenced exit fired
its cross-fade 250ms after resigning focus — a delay tuned on Android,
where imePadding moves frame-locked with the IME and 250ms genuinely means
settled. iOS declares 0.25s but dismisses its keyboard on a spring whose

idempotent so whichever arrives first acts alone.

reads well there. Two mechanisms, one principle: the second motion starts
when the first has provably finished, not when a timer hopes it has.

stranded at the top, on a physical iPhone 16e but never on a simulator. The
detent machinery kept getting blamed; it was a bad measurement.

The first layout pass after a sheet is presented measures the body before the
sheet has geometry. Instrumented on an iPhone 17 Pro: the body comes back

the real 402pt width every line of text wraps about three times over, so the

genuinely tall content at accessibility text sizes free to exceed the screen and
scroll, which is what the ceiling is for.

and a selection the set does not contain is invalid — which UIKit also answers
by opening the sheet full height. Seeding the selection narrowed that window;
keeping the old selection a member of the set closes it. At rest both are the
same value, so the set stays single-element and the sheet is not draggable.

symmetric cross-dissolve left both sets of rows legible at once and read as a

step change animates: the height also changes as one step's measurement settles,

every content-fit sheet in the app visibly grow as it opens. Mid-resize the
detent set keeps every step's last-known height, because a selection change only

Typography: reify the type system in code on both platforms (#288)

* Typography: reify the type system in code on both platforms

The type system existed only in prose. DESIGN.md documented nine roles;
iOS reified none of them and Android's theme was a bare `Typography()`.
Every refinement since landed at a call site, so it drifted — 465 iOS
`.font()` calls across ~65 distinct specs, and six sizes serving one
amount role.

The four defects that produced:

1. The same number wore two typefaces. The home balance was SF Pro Bold
   53pt; the amount you type one screen later was SF Pro *Rounded*
   SemiBold 64pt. Keypad digits were a third treatment, not tabular.
2. Android's biggest numbers had broken leading. `displayMedium` is 45sp
   with a 52sp line box, so `copy(fontSize = 64.sp)` rendered 64sp type
   in a 52sp box — a 0.81x ratio that crops the glyph. Every `fontSize`
   override in the app orphaned its line height, because `.copy()` makes
   that the easy thing to write.
3. The unit was undesigned. "21,000 sat" set the unit at the same size,
   weight and ink as the digits — about a third of the lockup carrying
   none of the information.
4. Display type ran at body tracking, while the overline was copy-pasted
   six times, five of them at 0.1em against a documented 0.06em, frozen
   in points so it was correct at exactly one text size.

What this adds:

- A role layer per platform. A role carries font, weight, tracking,
  casing and numeric treatment as one value — those travelling
  separately is how a call site came to take the size and forget the
  tracking, or the tabular figures and forget the digit transition.
- One amount ladder, four rungs, identical across platforms. Balance and
  live entry share `amountHero` because they are the same object.
- `AmountParts` splits value from unit so a hero can subordinate the unit
  on three axes. One `Text` with several runs, so autoscale scales them
  together rather than letting the ratio drift on long amounts.
- Reserved heights derived from resolved type metrics. Constant within a
  text size, so a unit swap still cannot reflow the canvas; growing with
  it, so large text is not cropped. The old 18pt status slot held a
  `.body` whose line box is ~22pt — it was clipping at the default size.
- Geist Sans + Geist Mono on Android (SIL OFL 1.1, attributed in
  Settings → Licenses), with the slashed zero via `ss09` for mnemonics
  and hex. iOS stays on SF Pro: SF Symbols are metrically bound to it and
  system-presented surfaces cannot be restyled.
- `TypographyGuardTest`, with an empty allowlist. A bare `fontSize`
  override or a literal `letterSpacing` now fails the build. It caught
  four real offenders on its first run.

Also fixed along the way: the fiat sub-balance was the one branch of its
ZStack with no styling at all, rendering in primary ink and skipping
tabular figures; and `AnimatedBalanceView.swift` — which DESIGN.md cited
as where the balance spec lived — turned out to be entirely dead.

Android 515 tests green; iOS green excluding the suites that need a live
local mint.

Hug the content in every iOS content-fit sheet (#281)

The zero-balance Send sheet and the Add Mint sheet opened at ~70% of the
screen with their content floating in a large void, where Android's
equivalents hug their content.

Every partial-height sheet derives its detent from a height measured inside
that same sheet, which closes a loop: measured height -> detent -> sheet
height -> the height proposed back to the content. Because the chrome
allowance nearly matched the real chrome, the loop was neutrally stable and
settled wherever the first layout pass left it -- roughly full-screen, during
the presentation transition -- and never recovered.

A ScrollView proposes nil height to its content, so a view measured inside
one always reports its ideal size regardless of how tall the sheet currently
is. That breaks the loop, and it predicted exactly which sheets were broken:
the three that measured inside a ScrollView were fine, and the two that
measured a bare view latched.

Replace four hand-rolled copies of the mechanism with one pair of modifiers:

  contentFitMeasured { ... }   // inside the NavigationStack, owns the ScrollView
  contentFitDetent(height)     // on the sheet root, owns the arithmetic

Breaking the measurement loop is necessary but not sufficient. The body's
height is reported more than once as layout settles -- a transient value, then
the real one, milliseconds apart. Handing presentationDetents a fresh
single-element set does not move the sheet: UIKit resolves the new set but
keeps whichever detent it had already selected, so the transient wins and the
final measurement is silently ignored. Instrumented on an iPhone 17 Pro,
0 -> 469 -> 241pt arrived within 70ms and the sheet stayed on the 547pt detent
instead of settling on 319pt. Binding the selection alongside the set removes
that race: the sheet is told which detent to be on, not merely which exist.

ContentFitSheetMetrics is now the single place the arithmetic lives:

  detent = content + navigationBar (44, when present) + bottomSafeArea

Notably absent is any allowance for the drag indicator.
presentationDragIndicator draws the grabber as an overlay over the content's
own top padding, so reserving height for it never moved the content down --
it landed as dead space at the bottom. The old flat 108pt constant carried
20pt of that plus 10pt of slack. Removing both tightens every sheet by 30pt.
The bottom safe area is resolved per device rather than assumed, so
home-button iPhones no longer over-shoot by 34pt, and the detent is clamped
to 90% of the screen so accessibility text sizes scroll inside the sheet
instead of silently pinning it full-height.

Onboarding's "What is ecash?" sheet joins the same mechanism. It hosts no
NavigationStack, hence the navigationBar flag. It loses its second .large
detent: the ScrollView and the clamp cover the large-text case that detent
existed for, and every other content-fit sheet is single-detent.

One connect-a-mint sheet for both platforms (#274)

* One connect-a-mint sheet for both platforms

Adding a first mint was four destinations with three copy variants, split
unevenly across iOS and Android. Collapse the wallet-home "Add mint" CTA and the
Send-with-no-mints face onto a single surface: a curated shortlist to tap, with
custom-URL entry and Nostr discovery pushed as steps inside the same sheet.

Recognition over recall — the old Android path dumped users on the Mints tab to
type a URL from memory.

Shared surface
- Context-aware header: from Send the sheet stays titled "Send" and carries the
  "Connect a mint first" headline explaining why the flow stalled; from "Add
  mint" the title says it already, so the headline is dropped rather than
  stacking a third level of title above the list.
- "Add custom mint URL" pushes an in-sheet "Add Mint" step; back returns to the
  picker. On iOS this replaces a button that opened the Nostr *discovery* list
  instead of a URL field — the label lied.
- "Discover mints" pushes the discovery list, and is not composed at all when
  WebSockets are off, so it can never dead-end on "WebSockets Required".

Typography
The old sheet stacked six type sizes and put the row title (15pt) below the
paragraph above it (16pt), ranking the tappable items under the prose. Down to
four sizes: row title and subtitle now share a size and separate by weight and
colour. One 20pt gutter for every element, hairlines moved from mid-avatar to
the text column, and 24pt above the section header so it stops gluing to the
paragraph. Section tracking is now @ScaledMetric (0.06em per DESIGN.md) instead
of an absolute value that ignored Dynamic Type. Footer links carry their own
vertical padding so they keep 44pt hit targets.

Android parity
- Send is enabled without a mint; it opens the surface instead of sitting dead.
- The "No mint" chip is gone — iOS emits nothing there. Gated on the Box, not
  its content, so no 14dp ghost gap survives above the balance.
- New WalletFlow.ConnectMint hosts it in the shell sheet, so the URL step can
  hand off to the camera through WalletFlowHandoffCoordinator (overlays render
  under the sheet's dialog window).

Also drops the nickname field from both Add Mint forms: it was collected and
silently discarded on each platform.

Out of scope and unchanged: the mint-chip menu and the Mints tab "Add mint" row,
which still open the standalone sheets.

* Keep the connect-a-mint sheet on the system's elevated background

The compact sheet was applying .canvasSheetBackground(), which resolves
systemBackground at .base elevation — the same pure black as the wallet canvas
in dark mode. A sheet that hugs its content floats *over* the screen, so it
dissolved into the background with only a rounded corner separating the two.

Every other partial-height sheet in the app already keeps the system background
(Mints list → Add Mint, Receive Ecash, and the Send sheet's compact face); the
flat canvas is for sheets that fill the screen, where matching the background is
right because the sheet replaces it. This was the only exception.

Promote that rule to a named modifier, canvasSheetBackground(whenFillingScreen:),
and retire UnifiedSendSheetBackground, which was a private duplicate of it.

* Let the pushed Add Mint step hug its content

The URL step was sent to `.large` on the theory that the keyboard needed the
room. It doesn't — iOS lifts a content-fit sheet above the keyboard, and the
field, submit button and paste link all stay reachable. What `.large` actually
bought was a band of dead space, because the form was a greedy `List` with its
buttons pinned by `safeAreaInset`.

It also diverged from Android, where the same step is a wrap-content column, and
it put two visual systems inside one sheet: flat canvas rows in the picker, then
an inset-grouped card in the step pushed on top of it.

Rebuild the form as an intrinsic-height column matching Android's
`AddMintFormBody`, report its height, and hug it in every host. Only the
discovery step still fills the sheet — it hosts a scrolling list and needs
bounded height.

The Mints-tab sheet shares this form, so it hugs now too; its detents move from
the call site into `AddMintSheet` alongside the measurement.

* Size the ecash concept sheet to its content on iOS

The sheet sat at a fixed `.medium` detent -- roughly half the screen,
independent of how much copy it holds -- with a `Spacer()` above the
CTA. The Spacer absorbed whatever was left over, so the gap between the
last paragraph and "Got it" was residue rather than a designed value,
and it grew with device height: ~107pt on iPhone 17e, ~115pt on
iPhone 17, ~134pt on iPhone 11.

Measure the content and drive a `.height()` detent from it, so the sheet
hugs its copy. The copy-to-button gap is now 24pt by construction on
every device and at every text size. `.large` stays in the detent set so
very large accessibility sizes can expand past the measured height
rather than clip.

wraps its content after the CTA-clipping fix, so iOS was the odd one
out. Verified on iPhone 11, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17 at XXL Dynamic
Type -- the sheet grows with the text and the CTA stays fully visible.

  a max fill past the balance) and clearer copy for the rare case where
  an exact amount fits the balance but the change-swap fee doesn't.

send max with includeFee: false confirms with fee 0 and the receiver
nets 87, while the old includeFee: true fails with "Insufficient
funds" — the original bug.

* crash: guard background mint writes against 0xdead10cc

TestFlight build 8 feedback reports the app "crashing" when a mint is
offline and when backgrounded. The wallet DB is SQLite, and two paths
write it autonomously during the background transition with no
background-task protection: the Nostr Cashu-request claim and the NPC
auto-claim. A SQLite lock held across suspension is the textbook trigger
for an iOS 0xdead10cc termination, which testers experience as a crash.

- Add withBackgroundWriteAssertion(): holds a UIKit background-task
  assertion across an async wallet-DB write so iOS grants a grace window
  to finish instead of suspending mid-write; always released via defer.
- Wrap the Nostr claim (receiveCashuRequestPayment) and NPC mint
  (mintNPCQuote) writes in the assertion.
- Stop the NPC/price pollers on .background and re-arm them on .active
  so no fresh mint network + DB write kicks off during the transition.

Probabilistic fix (no crash log was recoverable); hardens the exact
paths an offline mint + backgrounding exercise.

* receive: recover from stale NUT-13 counter ("Blinded Message is already signed")

A receive-swap derives blinded outputs deterministically from the keyset
counter (NUT-13). When that counter is behind what the mint has already signed
for the seed (reused seed + fresh/reset CDK DB), the mint rejects the swap. The
existing retry loop only matched Nutshell's "Duplicate outputs" wording, so
macadamia's "Blinded Message is already signed" fell straight through to the
generic "mint rejected" screen.

- TokenService: broaden isDuplicateOutputsError -> isCounterDesyncError (matches
  "duplicate outputs" / "already signed" / "outputs already signed"), and on the
  first collision run a one-shot wallet.restore() to fast-forward the counter
  past already-signed indices before retrying. No CDK changes.
- WalletErrors: honest, non-terminal fallback copy so "Try Again" re-runs the
  recovery instead of steering users to another mint.
- Tests: unit tests pinning isCounterDesyncError; a live-mint integration test
  reproducing the shared-seed collision and proving restore() clears it.

* crash: guard background mint writes against 0xdead10cc

TestFlight build 8 feedback reports the app "crashing" when a mint is
offline and when backgrounded. The wallet DB is SQLite, and two paths
write it autonomously during the background transition with no
background-task protection: the Nostr Cashu-request claim and the NPC
auto-claim. A SQLite lock held across suspension is the textbook trigger
for an iOS 0xdead10cc termination, which testers experience as a crash.

- Add withBackgroundWriteAssertion(): holds a UIKit background-task
  assertion across an async wallet-DB write so iOS grants a grace window
  to finish instead of suspending mid-write; always released via defer.
- Wrap the Nostr claim (receiveCashuRequestPayment) and NPC mint
  (mintNPCQuote) writes in the assertion.
- Stop the NPC/price pollers on .background and re-arm them on .active
  so no fresh mint network + DB write kicks off during the transition.

Probabilistic fix (no crash log was recoverable); hardens the exact
paths an offline mint + backgrounding exercise.

fix: use CDK default on-chain mint splits (#36)

On-chain minting used the requested quote amount as the CDK split target.
When a quote was overpaid, CDK repeated that quote-sized split across the
full credited amount. For example, a 2555 sat quote with 504662 sats paid
expanded to 1780 blinded outputs and exceeded the mint max_outputs limit.

Use CDK's default split target for mint issuance on iOS and Android so the
wallet does not force repeated quote-sized output groups for on-chain credits.

* Fix Receive screen showing 0 sat for IDv2 keyset tokens

parseToken() was summing proofs from token.proofsSimple(), but that API
is documented as "simplified - no keyset filtering" and TokenService
already has a comment noting it fails for IDv2 keyset tokens — it
passes an empty keyset list to token.proofs() which can't resolve the
short ID, so the call returns no proofs and the amount totals to 0.

Switch to token.value() which is the canonical "total value of the
token" API and computes the sum directly in the Rust core regardless
of keyset format.

Note: TokenService.calculateReceiveFee() and checkTokenSpendable() also
use proofsSimple() and likely silently misreport fee/spent state for
IDv2 tokens — leaving those for a follow-up since they need a different
fix (the proper proofs(mintKeysets:) API with wallet keysets).
